  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "B names a payer with sourced price anchors: ClaireMed at $99/provider/month and S10.AI at $99–$500/provider/month, both linked. A states outright that 'No one is currently shown paying' for Free Pascal/Lazarus documentation. A paying customer within 90 days is the goal, so this is the deciding factor.",
    "Even B's own counter-evidence shows physicians paying. Cydoc reached four paying customers and $27,900 in revenue. A cites no transaction of any kind in its market.",
    "B's case for proposes a narrow scope a solo builder could ship: an intake-to-note-draft layer that the physician pastes into an existing EHR. This scope directly avoids the $4–6k per-practice integration cost that sank the precedent. It also follows a buyer signal from that precedent, where the physician only wanted the note-drafting piece.",
    "A's own case against undercuts its premise in two ways. It says the Foundation funds development, not docs. It also cites a 2012 thread suggesting the blocker is maintainer engagement rather than tooling, which an outside product cannot fix.",
    "A's competitors are free and entrenched: the wiki, official docs, PasDoc, and free OSS tiers on Read the Docs and GitBook. That leaves little room for a paid tier.",
    "B carries real risk that keeps this from being a clear win. It requires a BAA with each customer and ongoing HIPAA safeguards. It recommends conference booths costing $3,000–$10,000 as the acquisition channel. Physicians may also distrust liability-bearing AI notes. A, however, has no evidenced path to revenue at all."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's payer and price hypothesis. The ~$50/month business tier is anchored only to Read the Docs' generic Business pricing. No source shows any company shipping Lazarus-based products paying for, or asking for, hosted or high-SLA Pascal documentation. The demand quotes, dated 2010, about 2014, and 2024, show frustration, not willingness to pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate. B wins mainly because A has no payer evidence. B's own demand evidence is thin: one Reddit anecdote about intake paperwork, and an AMA statistic relayed through competitor marketing. B's closest precedent failed with only four customers, and the brief gives no linked source for the Cydoc postmortem figures. B's 90-day path also depends on the narrowed, non-integrated scope and on clearing HIPAA/BAA setup quickly. Neither of these is evidenced, only argued."
}
